--- title: "Poisson Model" description: "Modeling count data, such as the number of events occurring in a fixed interval of time or space." categories: [Regression, Count Data, GLM] image: "Figures/7.png" order: 7 reading-time: true --- ## General Principles To model the relationship between a count outcome variable—e.g., counts of events occurring in a fixed interval of time or space—and one or more independent variables, we can use the _Poisson model_. This is a special shape of the binomial distribution; it is useful because it models binomial events for which the number of trials $n$ is unknown or uncountably large. ## Considerations ::: callout-caution - We have the same considerations as for [Regression for a continuous variable](1. Linear Regression for continuous variable.qmd). - We have the second [link function 🛈]{#linkF}: _log_. The _log_ link ensures that _λ_ is always positive. - The dependent variable in a Poisson regression must be a non-negative count. - To invert the log link function and linearly model the relationship between the predictor variables and the log of the mean rate parameter, we can apply the $exponential$ function (see comment in code). - A key assumption of the $Poisson$ distribution is that the mean and variance of the count variable are equal. If the variance is greater than the mean, a condition known as overdispersion, a [Gamma-Poisson model](9. Gamma-Poisson.qmd) might be more appropriate. ::: ## Example Below is an example code snippet demonstrating a Bayesian Poisson model using the BayesForge (BF) package. Data consist of: 1) A continuous dependent variable *total_tools*, which represents the number of tools produced by a civilization. 2) A continuous independent variable *population* representing population size. 3) A categorical independent variable *cid* representing different civilizations. The goal is to estimate the production of tools based on population size, accounting for each civilization. This example is based on @mcelreath2018statistical. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ### Python ::: {#ce5f8782 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from BayesForge import bf import jax.numpy as jnp # Setup device------------------------------------------------ m = bf(platform='cpu') # import data ------------------------------------------------ data_path = m.load.kline(only_path = True) m.data(data_path, sep=';') m.df["population"] = jnp.log(jnp.array(m.df.population.values, dtype=jnp.float64)) m.scale(['population']) m.df["cid"] = (m.df.contact == "high").astype(int) def model(cid, population, total_tools): a = m.dist.normal(3, 0.5, shape=(2,), name='a') b = m.dist.normal(0, 0.2, shape=(2,), name='b') l = jnp.exp(a[cid] + b[cid]*population) m.dist.poisson(l, obs=total_tools) # Run sampler ------------------------------------------------ m.fit(model, progress_bar=False) # Diagnostic ------------------------------------------------ m.summary() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` An NVIDIA GPU may be present on this machine, but a CUDA-enabled jaxlib is not installed. Scale log-population m$df["cid"] = as.integer(ifelse(m$df$contact == "high", 1, 0)) # Manipulate m$data_to_model(list('total_tools', 'population', 'cid')) # Send to model (convert to jax array) # Define model ------------------------------------------------ model <- function(total_tools, population, cid){ # Parameter prior distributions a = m$dist$normal(3, 0.5, name='a', shape = reticulate::tuple(2L)) b = m$dist$normal(0, 0.2, name='b', shape = reticulate::tuple(2L)) l = jnp$exp(a[cid] + b[cid]*population) # Likelihood m$dist$poisson(l, obs = total_tools, name = "total_tools") } # Run MCMC ------------------------------------------------ m$fit(model) # Optimize model parameters through MCMC sampling # Summary ------------------------------------------------ m$summary() # Get posterior distribution ``` ### Julia ```julia using PyBayesForge # Setup device------------------------------------------------ m = importBF(platform="cpu") # Import Data & Data Manipulation ------------------------------------------------ data_path = m.load.kline(only_path = true) m.data(data_path, sep=';') m.df["population"] = jnp.log(jnp.array(m.df.population.values)) m.scale(["population"]) # Normalize log-population m.df["cid"] = m.df.contact.eq("high").astype("int") # Define model ------------------------------------------------ @BF function model(cid, population, total_tools) a = m.dist.normal(3, 0.5, shape=(2,), name="a") b = m.dist.normal(0, 0.2, shape=(2,), name="b") l = jnp.exp(a[cid] + b[cid]*population) m.dist.poisson(l, obs=total_tools) end # Run mcmc ------------------------------------------------ m.fit(model) # Optimize model parameters through MCMC sampling # Summary ------------------------------------------------ m.summary() # Get posterior distributions ``` ::: ## Mathematical Details In the Bayesian formulation, we define each parameter with [priors 🛈]{#prior}. We can express the Bayesian regression model accounting for prior distributions as follows: $$ Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i) $$ $$ log(\lambda_i) = \alpha + \beta X_i $$ $$ \alpha \sim \text{Normal}(0, 1) $$ $$ \beta \sim \text{Normal}(0, 1) $$ Where: - $Y_i$ is the dependent variable for observation *i*. - $\log()$ is the **log link function**. This function links the log of the mean of the response variable, $\lambda_i$, to the linear predictor, $\alpha + \beta X_i$. The logarithm is the canonical link function for the Poisson distribution. It ensures that the predicted mean, $\lambda_i = \exp(\alpha + \beta X_i)$, will always be positive, as required for a Poisson rate parameter. - $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the intercept and regression coefficient, respectively, with their associated prior distributions. - $X_i$ is the value of the independent variable for observation *i*. ## Model validation tests - [Comparison with Stan](https://github.com/BGN-for-ASNA/BF/tree/main/Test/4.%20Rethinking/Numpyro%20backend): `6.Poisson.py` fits the same model with BayesForge and Stan and compares the posterior distributions (KL divergence). - [Documentation examples](https://github.com/BGN-for-ASNA/BF/tree/main/Test/3.Documentation): the Python, R and Julia examples of this page are run by the documentation tests (`Python/test_model_pages.py`, `R/test_r_model_pages.py`, `Julia/test_julia_model_pages.py`). ## Notes ::: callout-note - We can apply multiple variables similarly to [chapter 2](2. Multiple continuous variables.qmd). - We can apply interaction terms similarly to [chapter 3](3. Interaction between continuous variables.qmd). - We can apply categorical variables similarly to [chapter 4](4. Categorical variable.qmd). ::: ## Reference(s) ::: {#refs} :::
